name: Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park
blurb: ʻŌhiʻa rainforest, honeycreepers and the introduced predators that threaten them.

tip.title: Let ʻōhiʻa die back
tip.text: Rapid ʻŌhiʻa Death kills ʻōhiʻa trees. Set ʻŌhiʻa lehua to -100% and watch the nectar-feeding honeycreepers, the moths, and the predators further up.

sources.title: National Park Service: Hawaiʻi Volcanoes nature

notes: The species list comes from GBIF occurrence records inside a circle around the park, so it can include nearby areas. Feeding links come from GloBI records and the sources listed where they state them; others are general ecology and are illustrative.

nodes.desc: The most common native tree in Hawaiʻi and often the first to take root on fresh lava. Its nectar feeds honeycreepers, and the fungus behind Rapid ʻŌhiʻa Death threatens it on the Big Island.
A low native shrub of the volcano slopes whose berries are eaten by birds and the nene.
Introduced omnivore, mostly plant-eating, that roots up the forest floor. The park lists feral pigs among the introduced animals harming its wildlife.

nodes.name: Nēnē
nodes.desc: Hawaiʻi's state bird, a goose that grazes the leaves, seeds, fruit and flowers of grasses and shrubs on lava and shrubland. Introduced mongooses, pigs and cats cut it to 30 birds by 1952.
A red honeycreeper that feeds mainly on ʻōhiʻa nectar and also gleans moths and spiders from the canopy. It carries bird malaria, spread by introduced mosquitoes.
Caterpillars chew native leaves and adult moths are a main food of hoary bats and insect-eating birds.
Introduced omnivore that eats fruit, seeds and eggs. It is prey for hawks, cats and mongooses.

nodes.name: Hawaiian hoary bat
nodes.desc: The islands' only native land mammal. It hunts at night, mainly eating moths and beetles, and roosts in trees such as ʻōhiʻa. Federally endangered.
Introduced predator, the most recorded mammal in this area. It eats insects, rodents and birds and raids ground nests of birds that evolved without mammal predators.

nodes.name: Feral cat
nodes.desc: Introduced top predator with no natural enemy here. It preys on native birds, nesting nene and rodents.
Drives plant growth from the sea-level coast to the high summit.
Break down dead leaves, fern trunks and carcasses, returning nutrients to the soil.
